content.thinking:
I'm putting together the postmortem and sorting out the timeline. The incident seems to start at 23:23, when the P1 flag was switched on by an admin. There's a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py that's been firing from 23:23 to 23:30, and I'm checking how the flag's partial rollout lines up with that window.

Argus has acted, and the revert didn't take effect within the window: the P1 flag still showed as on at 23:30, even after it was switched off at 23:29:13. That refutes the flag-revert hypothesis, so I'm putting the flag back on for now. For earlier causes, the only change in the record before onset is P1, and the deploy check came back empty, which is absence of evidence rather than a ruled-out deploy.

I'm checking whether the earlier changes could be the cause: the service was measured healthy before onset, and no deploy turned up in the window read, so the running revision looks unlikely. The flag is still showing as on at 23:30 even after the revert, so the revert may not have reached the service.

I'm tracing the causal chain: page requests hit a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 from 23:23, which the page handler turned into a failed page. The monthly-spend flag that was switched on at 23:23:44 routed evaluations into that path. The division itself is the open part, since the trace confirms the error at line 47 but not what is being divided.

I'm checking whether the monthly-spend path is actually what breaks: the trace shows the ZeroDivisionError at line 47, but nothing yet confirms that the divisor is the count of this month's purchases. I'm also noting that the postmortem should flag the missing test for shoppers with no purchases this month, since the fixture only covers the ordinary case.

I'm weighing whether to propose a staged rollout as a contributing factor, since the flag went from partial to fully on within about a minute with no hold in between.

I'm weighing a staged rollout with automatic rollback on an error rise as a fix, since the flag went from off to on for every evaluation at once and I don't see a staged rollout in the record. I'm also looking at whether anyone was paged, since the alert fired but no on-call incident is linked to it.

I'm weighing whether to flag the flag's evaluations still showing on at 23:30 as a factor that held before the incident, since the record doesn't show whether caching or propagation delay caused it, so I'll leave that question to the why-it-did-not-help and what-went-wrong sections.

I'm reconsidering how to word the went-wrong part: the revert was judged refuted and undone even though the service's own 23:30 log still showed the flag on, so it's unclear whether the revert ever reached the service. I also notice this matches the earlier incident, where the same flag was tried and refuted, and Argus tried it again anyway.

I'm going through the went-well items now: the investigator's timing of the start at 23:23 against the flag toggle, the Mitigation Agent's revert that could be put back, and the Code-Fix draft PR. I'm weighing whether the Mitigation Agent putting the flag back on is a good result, since that's debatable.

I'm drafting the action items now and checking each contributing factor against them. For the flag-gated path, I'd add a check that runs its tests with the flag on, including the case of shoppers with no purchases this month, before the flag can be switched on in production. I'll also roll out monthly-spend-style flags in stages to a small share of shoppers with a hold that watches the account page error rate, and link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page.

I'm now working out the two remaining sections of the postmortem: what to do to stop the harm, and why the revert did not help. For stopping the harm, I'm planning to switch the monthly-spend flag off again and confirm in the service's own logs that every evaluation reports it off, that the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 stops, and that the account page error rate drops back to its level before the incident. For why the revert did not help, I'm going to trace how and when the service picks up flag changes from the provider, and if it did receive the change, work out why the error still happened.

I'm checking which figure to use for the 23:30 log line, and I'll cite it by its label rather than writing the digits in the prose. The revert's failure to reach the service is the open question I'm handing off to the why-it-did-not-help section. Going forward, the main risk is that account pages keep failing for shoppers with no purchases this month while the flag stays on, so I'm writing that up as the still-at-risk point.

I'm drafting the root-cause section now: the failing path runs through a monthly spend average that divides by a count of this month's purchases, which evaluates to zero for shoppers with no purchases yet this month.

Now I'm checking how the division is built in the monthly spend code: the total gets divided by the count of this month's purchases, and that count can be empty for a shopper who has bought before but not yet this month.

I'm checking the deploy history and the flag provider's change log for the hour before the incident. No deploy came back in the window, and all replicas were running one revision that was measured healthy before the flag switched on. The only other flag change in that hour came from Argus.

Checking the flag history and the deploy record for the hour before the incident, I'm confirming that the only flag change came from Argus and that the revision all replicas ran was measured healthy before the switch.

I'm checking the citations for the root cause and the ruled-out deploy, and I'm noting the assumptions: the revert's failure rests on the flag not reaching the service, and the affected shoppers rest on the failing path reading.

Marking the root-cause section's fields as resolved: the causal chain reaches a cause, and that cause rests on a reading that was not run. For the nobody-paged factor, I'm noting that an on-call engineer working alongside Argus could have caught the escalation with no explanation left. Checking the action items against the contributing factors, the test gap has no fix listed yet.

Checking the remaining contributing factors against the action items: the first one has no addressing action, and the other two aren't covered by any fix either.

action_items.item: Before a feature flag can be switched on in production, run the tests of the code path it enables with the flag on, including the cases the test fixtures mark as ordinary, such as a shopper with no purchases this month.
Roll out io-shop feature flags in stages, starting with a small share of shoppers, and hold at each stage on the account page error rate so the rollout stops and reverts when the rate rises.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service's error rate over all requests rose well above its usual level.

Account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at line {F1.1} from the onset minute onward. According to Code-Fix's reading of the source, `serve_account_page` catches that exception and returns a failed page.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, or the one revision all replicas run: no deploy came back over the window read before the onset. With that revision in place and the flag off, the service was measured healthy, with account pages rendering normally and its error rate at its usual level.
Any other flag change: the flag provider's history showed only the one change by someone other than Argus in the hour read, the switch of monthly-spend-feature to on.

causal_chain.step: An admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. Before that the service evaluated the flag off every time. In the onset minute some evaluations came back on, and from {Gce95.4} every evaluation was on, which sent account pages down the monthly spend-summary path. Switching the flag off did not end the failures, but that does not clear the flag: the service's own log in the minute after the revert ({Gce95.5}) still showed every evaluation on, so the revert was not seen to reach the service.
According to Code-Fix's reading, the monthly spend-summary path fails for any shopper who has bought before but has made no purchase in the current month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An administrator switched on a feature that sent shoppers' account pages through a new monthly spending summary, and that summary's calculation failed and took the page down with it, likely for shoppers who had bought before but had not bought anything yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: Before monthly-spend-feature was switched on in production, no check was seen that ran the path it enables against a shopper with past purchases and none this month. The test file's own fixture calls that the ordinary case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The ZeroDivisionError would have shown up in testing before the flag was switched on, and the flag would not have reached shoppers with the fault in place.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for every evaluation at once. No staged rollout and no hold watching the account page error rate were seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of shoppers would have reached the failing path, and the rise in failed pages could have stopped the rollout before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to an on-call page, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been working the incident while Argus did. When Argus ran out of explanations and escalated with the flag back on, someone could have kept the flag off and confirmed it reached the service, instead of the failures carrying on.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent dated the onset to the minute the flag was switched on and named the flag change, with the failing line, as the candidate cause.
The Mitigation Agent switched monthly-spend-feature off, an action that could be put back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: The flag revert was judged refuted and monthly-spend-feature was switched back on, even though the service's own log for the minute after the revert still showed every evaluation on. So it was never settled whether the revert reached the service, and switching the flag back on restored the state that set the failures off.

The second investigation formed again the same flag candidate that had already been refuted. It looked no further at why the revert had not shown at the service, and the incident was left with no explanation to act on.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `render_spend_summary` calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month`, which divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases made in the current month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month there are no such purchases, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, and `serve_account_page` turns that exception into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature switched back on, account pages could keep failing for shoppers who have bought before but have bought nothing this month.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. Confirm at the service that its own log lines report the flag off for every evaluation, that the ZeroDivisionError lines from src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stop, and that the error rate over all requests falls back to its level before the incident, {series_before}.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out whether switching monthly-spend-feature off at {P2.1} reached io-shop at all, given that the service's log in the minute after ({Gce95.5}) still showed every evaluation on. To do that, trace how and when io-shop picks up a flag change from the flag provider. If the change did reach the service, find out why the account page failures carried on.
